messages.subject: Failure to compute overdispersion
parts:
Hello secr users,

I've recently been introduced to secr so am a novice - please bear with me if I asking seemingly stupid questions. I've been advised to use secr by reviewers and judging by the degree of flexibility and the type of models that can be performed, I'm excited to be working with this package.

So, I am working on a camera trap data set of a large and very rare wild cow in southeast Asia. Grids were used, and contained 36 camera trap stations at a spacing of 0.5km, with a grid cell size of 0.25km2 and a total area of 9km2. Three grids were ran, resulting in 27km2 total survey area within one forest. The distance between grids was 
~10km to avoid resampling of the same herds. They survey duration was 87 days per grid. The wild cattle were captured at only two out of three grids. Individuals were identified from natural markings, and I also have photos of individuals not identifiable. The true number of individuals were/are unknown.The sample size is very small. Grid 1 had 27 captures and 8 cows identified: cow 1 (3), cow 2 (3), cow 3 (3), cow 4 (3), cow 5 (4), cow 6 (4), cow 7 (2), cow 8 (5). Grid2 = no captures. Grid3 had 14 captures and 8 cows identified: cow 9 (1), cow 10 (1), cow 11 (1), cow 12 (1). cow 13 (2), cow 14 (2), cow 15 (2). cow 16 (4). I do not have covariates to include for these models. 

I am looking to run multiple models simulating differing degrees of identification: 1) identified cows and omitting unidentifiable individuals, 2) identified cows included unidentifiable cows, and 3) no identification of cows. 

I'm currently addressing 1) so I'm trialing 'Model 3, sighting-only data with unknown number of marks' and have identified a stable buffer but have been unable to run simulations to compute overdispersion as, after a great deal of time (~30 mins) it returns the error message: "Error in (function(f,p, ...,hessian=FALSE, typsize=rep(1, legnth(p)), :  invalid function value in 'nlm' optimizer. 

I was looking to run the same test using the example data set (to at least see the output and compare input files) but I've not been able to find the right one (MRCH). I have tried running another example 'Stoats' but I get the same error back.

I have searched both forums for guidance on this issue but have not made any headway, so here I am....and my questions are:

Can anyone tell me what this error message mean? How can I overcome it to compute overdispersion and test model fit? 
Can anyone point me in the direction of the MRCH example data set?

If you've had the patience to sit this out and read my message then I am very thankful.

Junglemadjane

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Failure to compute overdispersion
parts:
Hi JMJ


I am not optimistic that there is an easy solution. The error message is fairly generic, just indicating that likelihood maximisation crashed. There could be (i) problems in the software itself (the mark-resight part has undergone a major overhaul for the next version, expected in a few weeks), (ii) problems with small samples, or (iii) some error in the way you’ve set things up. Maybe all three.


I can at least provide some demo data files for secr-markresight.pdf (attached - they're just simulated, and may not be the same as used in the vignette). However, I would strongly advise that you hold off on analysing all-sighting data in secr 2.10, given that secr 3.0 is just around the corner (it’s coming first in pre-release form on the Density website).


I’ve a few other pedantic and dismal comments that won’t necessarily help, but here they are anyway:


1. Although in your mind you sampled grids of 36 squares, in practice what you did was to position cameras at points (perhaps at the centres or randomly within each square?). There is no real sense in which the area sampled was 9 sq km. There will be a convex polygon enclosing the outermost cameras, with area < 9 sq km, and another, unknown, area from which cows wandered in front of a camera.

2. I imagine you treated each day as a sampling occasion. That is excessive and slows things down unnecessarily. You can probably collapse all occasions down to 1 and use a ‘count’ detector type (preferably with detectfb = ‘HHN’), without losing information.

3. If you aim for an average density over all three grids then be sure to include a dummy line for Grid 2 in the capture file (using code ‘NONE’ for the animalID; see ?read.capthist).

4. It would help to have some hints regarding the extent of movements by individual cows, and whether they really move in herds (that clashes with a basic SECR assumption of independence, and probably means you have even less data than you thought).

5. Mark-resight is really no fun. Formally incorporating counts of sightings of unidentifiable cows requires that they are counted exactly as if they were identifiable – i.e. with equal probability of detection. My sense is that this is almost impossible to achieve (avoiding double counting etc.).


My suggestion is to do a standard SECR (not mark-resight) analysis of the data on identifiable animals and in your text apply an ad-hoc adjustment for the fraction of individuals that were identifiable – probably that’s what you meant to do anyway. If nothing else, the SECR analysis will give a clean estimate of sigma (if sigma large (>1km) or poorly estimated, further digging is a waste of time).


Murray
